It think it's stupid that "AI Bubble" gets used over and over. In infra names you have: 

- 1-3x fwd P/E memory companies from Samsung to $ESMT. With HBM players now having hyperscaler multi-year price floor LTAs. 

- Optical companies like $POET traded -$97M under net cash. Valuing the operating business very negatively, not even at $0. 

- While AI companies with larger premiums continue to record demand over the next 3-5 years. Such as the new $20B LTAs signed w/ $COHR to $5B LTAs signed w/ $LITE. 

Can someone in the media honestly see negative EV high-beta optical companies, where 2 years of burnrate would still value the company below $0.  

or single digit memory companies with contracted demand + price floors years out and say that's a bubble?

Many of these names are extremely profitable today... 

But obviously there's other elements inside the theme, such as: 

- Certain startups like Instinct that look like a private valuation bubble. 
- Leveraged Neoclouds that didn't finance properly
- and AI lab valuations and commitments, which should be viewed cautiously. 

But everything gets grouped into one with the boogyman of "leverage" or "debt". 

Yes, valuations can compress or correct from macro, potential regulatory uncertainty, or potential capex reductions. 

But for the companies physically powering the AI buildout, it looks more like the Great AI Deleveraging of 2026... 

Than anything like fundamental demand destruction.

As more earnings come out and free cash flow accumulates over time.

I'm confident in a recovery, especially in bottlenecks, and for markets to eventually discern durability + growth over frothy valuations tied to AI.

Various commentary from Qualcomm, Arm, to Meta executives this week during the AI selloff: 

$LITE CEO: "You had a comment from the CEO of $IREN and I'd second that. There's a massive disconnect in what we're seeing in our demand books. 

And what the markets are showing. And yet you're seeing a massive, massive selloff." (Fri, Nov 6)

$AMD CEO CNBC: "We're at the very beginning of the adoption cycle, where people can see where AI and superintelligence will take us" 

"We are seeing demand being higher than supply" (Wed, Nov 4)

$ARM CEO regarding a debate whether AI infrastructure spending is about to peak:

"I think in some states where it gets harder, other states may pick it up to make it easier, but I do believe strongly that if the US hesitates in any way shape performance in terms of data center buildout...

"The rest of the world is ready and willing. There is just huge demand for this capacity. And I think globally the US really wants to be able to compete against China. China is not slowing down at all." (Thu, Nov 5)

$APLD CEO: Bank construction lending, project financing and bond markets remain available, although interest rates and credit spreads have risen

"The big risk is delivering on time." "The demand picture is extremely robust." (Mon, Nov 2)

$QCOM CEO: "It's not demand bound. It's a supply bound." 

"We're short on wafers, we're short on substrate, we're short on assembly. Everything is short because demand is very, very high." 

"I think what the market is reacting to is what is the speed of the compute build out."

$META on political risk: "We did have a governor that won last night who did make data centers a big part of the platform.

Say as soon as we get past the inauguration, let's meet because we don't want to lose this investment in our town. We don't want these jobs to go elsewhere." (Wed, Nov 4)

Even politicians campaigning against data centers are negotiating. But Meta's president also emphasized that starting new US DCs will become more difficult. 

TLDR:
-> Extremely bullish commentary from accelerator players, networking, and semi companies
-> DC developers report strong pricing/demand, but increasingly emphasize financing, permitting and execution risks (more cautious)
-> Politicians that previously campaigned against DCs are showing cooperation

There's an important difference between demand disappearing and demand being delayed by the inability to build fast enough.

Despite the severity of the selloff, I'm not seeing evidence of widespread AI demand destruction in commentary.

I know this is a predictable opinion from me but I don't agree with the strong emotional reaction against the anti-data-center movements that I've seen this week.

As I see it, algorithmic progress means that whatever you would be able to do with more and bigger data centers in 2 years, you will be able to do with the data centers we have today in 4 years - probably sooner. So nothing remotely apocalyptically bad will happen from even extreme levels of success by anti-data-center people.

Meanwhile we need all the time we can get to better harden the world against both already-visible cybersecurity issues and any bio and other risks soon to come. Science applications are bottlenecked by many things other than AI, so slowing AI down by one year will slow those down by much less than one year.

Given this, a slowdown in compute hyper-scaling seems quite net good? Notice this is without any controversial "doomer arguments", RSI etc. Even if net-bad, it's certainly not worse than like 10+ other political things.

Expanding on why I believe "ETH as store of value (SoV)" makes much more sense to focus on than "ETH as fee-burning token".

Three primary reasons:

1. ETH as fee-burning token never was as strong as it seemed
2. Optimizing for ETH as fee-burning token would demand Ethereum and ETH function in ways that are very hard to make compatible with decentralization and capture resistance.
3. Meanwhile, optimizing for ETH as SoV is aligned with Ethereum focusing on its unique strengths (decentralization and CROPS)

EIP-1559 (including its burn) is fine and good, we should keep them. But we should not feel sad if fee burn is < 10% of breakeven indefinitely; the value of ETH comes from elsewhere.

The core idea: the big thing that people appreciate about Ethereum is decentralization and CROPS. The main pragmatic benefit that these things translate into is stability. SoV is the category where that is not an unneeded extra we merely put effort into for ideological reasons, but rather a pragmatic strength from the perspective of people putting in their assets. And in the era of AI disruption, stability will be highly valued.

2. Optimizing for ETH as fee-burning token would demand compromising decentralization and capture resistance

If we decide we actually want to optimize ETH for burning fees to justify a present-day ~$270B market cap, then Ethereum would essentially be functioning as a world-scale major corporation - it would be somewhere around L'Oreal (#55).

Now, what do *real* major corporations have to do in order to maintain their positions in the long term?

1. They spend. AI estimates L'Oreal as spending ~0.58% of its market cap per year on R&D. This would bankrupt the EF almost immediately. So this would require in-protocol funding to the tune of ~700k ETH per year, with all the political issues that it entails (so validator revenue would get cut by 2/3). And that's just R&D. Corporations have to spend on all kinds of things beyond just cranking out more units of their pre-existing product.
2. They govern. To survive new waves of technology and culture, you have to make highly opinionated choices to go after new markets, make new kinds of products with new features to appeal to people who think in new ways and use the newest technologies. Ethereum would need to have highly interventionist governance, for the long term.

Needless to say, both of these are far from conducive to optimizing capture resistance and decentralization.

On top of this there is another concern: optimizing for fee burning means optimizing for high gas prices to some degree. This may price out users, including some users who may need privacy and security the most. The price that maximizes price * usage leads to less usage than the price that allows as much usage as possible subject to safe blockchain resource limits.

3. Optimizing for ETH as SoV is aligned with decentralization and CROPS

Whenever I ask what people appreciate the most about Ethereum (as opposed to either other blockchains, or anything outside the blockchain world), the most common answer is: decentralization and CROPS (censorship and capture resistance, open source, privacy and security).

Decentralization and CROPS have a lot of value, even to institutions. For individuals, privacy is often viewed as an abstract ideology. For institutions, it's prudent risk management, data protection law compliance, and a number of other things. Likewise for security. And likewise for running your own node (enterprise buzzword: "on-prem deployment").

But what about for the ETH holder? Well, it depends why you're an ETH holder. If you want ETH to optimally chase financial trends and collect fees from them, then you want a Fearless Leader™ who bravely shouts on the socials that Ethereum loves [insert opportunity here] and will pragmatically reconfigure itself to give it explicit protocol support.

But if your primary reason to hold ETH is as an SoV, then you will be judging ETH by SoV-ish metrics. And what is the first and most important SoV-ish metric?

To survive.

That's what a big chunk of this last Devcon was about ("post-quantum and post-AI"). You want a chain that is taking conservative tradeoffs ("hash-only security, all formally proven, >3x more rounds than known to be necessary for security"). You want a chain that is aiming for at least partial ossification, where the great balance of work will move to higher levels of the stack once the core is complete. You want a chain that aims to minimize protocol politics, by having a very high bar before it accepts either precompiles that bloat the protocol or new kinds of in-protocol rewards that could get captured.

What other SoV'ish metrics?

The ability to easily hold it safely (hence, work on multisigs).
The ability to hold it privately (hence, kohaku work).
The ability to hold it privately *and* safely (hence, 8288 and private-AA workstreams already starting).
The guarantee that if you have coins, you can send them, and block builders can't stop you (FOCIL)
Minimized infrastructure dependence (basically the whole decentralization roadmap, including the fact that I am able to currently run a node on this laptop, and it synced in < 6 hours and takes up only 1/8 of my hard drive - better stats than in 2019!)

Now, are there "adoption" goals that are highly synergistic with SoV?

Very much so.

The more assets there are natively issued on L1, including both RWAs and native decentralized assets, the larger a set of things you can "do" with your ETH, the better. Being able to easily (including safely, trustlessly) convert back and forth between ETH and other assets, use ETH as collateral to do things with other assets, etc, all forms part of the utility of holding ETH.

There are still some conflicts between serving these use cases and decentralization (eg. we want to be careful about fast slots and impact on centralization), but on the whole much less than what you get if you maximize fees.

Conclusion:

The best social reason to care about Ethereum is because it makes decentralization and CROPS properties a reality for more people and uses.

The best private reason to hold ETH is its SoV properties, which are a direct consequence of that decentralization and CROPS.
